passages.title: The call to arise and warn
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Muddaththir opens on a man lying wrapped in a cloak — and the revelation that comes calls him to rise. These seven ayat are the beginning of the Prophet's ﷺ public mission: one address (ayah 1) followed by six commands (ayat 2–7) that together map the whole shape of the work ahead — go out and warn, proclaim the greatness of your Lord, keep yourself clean, keep away from idols, give without seeking more in return, and be patient. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān numbers them as exactly that: six injunctions. Taken as one unit, they read less like a list of instructions than like a commission handed over at the moment a man attained messengership.

## The silence before the call

Almost nothing in this passage lands properly until you know what came immediately before it.

Revelation had begun in the cave of Ḥirāʼ with **iqraʼ** — *Read! In the Name of your Lord Who has created* (96:1–5). Then, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, after a few ayat of that sūrah had come down, further revelation stopped for a period of time. That interval of silence has a name in the sciences of the Qurʼān: **fatrat al-waḥy**, the temporary cessation of revelation. And it is towards the end of that period that our sūrah arrives.

It is confirmed in **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī** and **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**, on the authority of Abū Salamah, that Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh reported hearing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ speak about the pause in revelation. The Prophet ﷺ said that while he was walking he heard a voice from the sky. He lifted his gaze towards the sky and saw the same angel who had come to him at the cave of Ḥirāʼ, sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth. He fled from him in fear until he fell down to the ground. Then he went to his family and said, *"Wrap me up, wrap me up"* — and they wrapped him up. So Allah revealed: **O you wrapped up! Arise and warn!** — until *And keep away*. And then, in the Prophet's ﷺ own words, the revelation started coming strongly and frequently in succession. The long silence was over.

Two details in that report are worth pausing on.

**First**, Ibn Kathīr draws a careful conclusion from the wording. The way the ḥadīth is narrated necessitates that revelation had descended before this — because of the Prophet's ﷺ statement, *"the same angel who had come to me at the cave of Ḥirāʼ."* That angel was Jibrīl, who had come to him with *iqraʼ*. After that first occurrence in the cave a period of time passed, and then the angel descended again. So al-Muddaththir is not the first revelation; it is the first after the pause. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded this ḥadīth by way of az-Zuhrī, and **Imām Aḥmad** recorded it from Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān with the fuller list of commands, through *And keep away from ar-Rujz*.

**Second**, notice what the man did. Under the weight of what he had seen he went home and asked to be covered — and the address that came to him is one Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes as affectionate and endearing.

### A second occasion: the feast of al-Walīd

**Aṭ-Ṭabarānī** recorded another report, from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah prepared some food for the Quraysh, and when they had eaten he asked them: *what do you have to say about this man?* They went round in circles — a magician, no; a soothsayer, no; a poet, no — until they eventually all agreed that it was magic from ancient times. When this news reached the Prophet ﷺ, he became grieved, covered his head and wrapped himself up. This, the report says, is when Allah revealed ayat 1 through 7.

Put the two reports side by side and the posture is the same: a man withdrawn under a cloak, once out of awe, once out of grief. And in both, the command that comes is the same — **qum**, *arise*.

## Which came first, al-Muzzammil or al-Muddaththir?

Because this sūrah stands so near the beginning, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that **some scholars considered it the first sūrah in order of revelation** — though according to the well-known authentic aḥādīth, the first instalment of revelation comprised the initial ayat of Sūrah Iqraʼ.

There is a related difference over its place relative to Sūrah al-Muzzammil. Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī cites a report from Jābir ibn Zayd that al-Muddaththir was revealed *after* al-Muzzammil, and some scholars attribute that narration to Ibn ʿAbbās as well. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues the other way: according to the narration from the two Ṣaḥīḥs, it is clear that the first sūrah revealed after the temporary cessation was al-Muddaththir — for had al-Muzzammil been revealed before it, Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh, the narrator of the ḥadīth, would have narrated it. Maʿārif's own conclusion is measured: the two forms of address are near-synonyms, so it is very likely both sūrahs were revealed in connection with the *same* incident — the voice from the sky, Jibrīl al-Amīn sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth, the return home and the wrapping in a mantle. Which set of ayat was revealed first is, it says, not clear.

What the two sūrahs do have is a division of labour, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: the injunctions at the beginning of **al-Muzzammil relate to the Prophet's ﷺ personal purification and perfection**; those at the beginning of **al-Muddaththir relate to preaching, propagation and human reform**. Inward first, then outward.

## Ayah 1: why "O you covered up in your clothes?"

The word **al-muddaththir** is derived from **dithār** — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the concrete image: a thick, warm over-garment, such as a cloak or mantle, which a person wears in winter over his other clothes to protect himself from cold. The outer layer you pull round yourself when you want the cold — and the world — kept at a distance.

And the address does not come by name, or by title, or by rebuke. It comes by the very state the man was in at that moment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the form of address is affectionate and endearing, as was explained under al-Muzzammil in the preceding sūrah — the two forms of address being near-synonyms.

## Ayah 2: "Arise and warn"

Then the address turns into a mission.

**Qum** — *arise*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān allows the word its primary sense first: *remove the additional clothes in which you have wrapped yourself*. And it says it is also not unlikely that *stand up* means *prepare yourself for the onerous task of reforming the creation of Allah*. Both readings are the same movement: from lying down to standing up, from private to public.

Ibn Kathīr glosses **fa-andhir** as: prepare to go forth with zeal and warn the people. And he makes a statement of the first importance — **with this the Prophet ﷺ attained messengership, just as he attained prophethood with the first revelation.**

The word **indhār** deserves care, because "warning" sounds harsh in English and the Arabic is not. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that indhār is a warning **based on love and affection** — such as a father's warning his children against the dangers of a snake, a scorpion or a fire. The prophets proclaim the divine message and warn its rejecters of the evil consequences of rejection; and so they have received the titles **nadhīr** and **bashīr**. A *nadhīr* is one who affectionately and endearingly warns people against harmful things; a *bashīr* is one who gives glad tidings. The Qurʼān has conferred both titles on the Prophet ﷺ, and the Book is replete with them.

So why does this ayah mention only warning? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers from the situation on the ground: at the time of the revelation of this ayah there were only a handful of Muslims. The rest of the people were all rejecters and disbelievers — they needed to be warned, and did not merit glad tidings.

## Ayah 3: "And magnify your Lord"

**Wa rabbaka fa-kabbir.** Ibn Kathīr's gloss is direct: to declare the greatness of Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands it: proclaim the greatness of your Lord **both orally and practically**.

Then it asks the question worth asking of any divine name in any ayah: why *Rabb* here? Because, it says, this attribute is itself the effective cause of the injunction — He is the **Sustainer, Cherisher and Nourisher of the entire world**. And **He alone is worthy of kibriyāʼ**, greatness. That is why the rendering reads *"revere your Lord ˹alone˺"*.

On the practical side, **takbīr** literally signifies saying *Allāhu Akbar*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this includes the **takbīr of taḥrīmah** — the opening *Allāhu Akbar* that begins the prayer — and the other takbīrs as well, and takbīr is recited outside the prayer too, as in the adhān and the iqāmah. But it is careful not to narrow the ayah: there is no indication in the Qurʼān that this injunction refers *specifically* to uttering *Allāhu Akbar* to commence the prayer.

Note the order, too. Magnifying Allah comes before purifying, before keeping away, before enduring.

## Ayah 4: "And purify your garments"

This is the ayah on which the early authorities differ most, and the differences are worth seeing in full, because they are not rival theories so much as layers of one meaning. Ibn Kathīr gathers them:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (reported by al-ʿAwfī): do not let the garments you wear be from earnings that are unlawful.
- It has also been said: do not wear your clothes in disobedience.
- **Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn**: clean them with water — the plain, literal sense.
- **Ibn Zayd**: the idolaters would not clean themselves, so Allah commanded him to clean himself and his garments. **This view was preferred by Ibn Jarīr.**
- **Saʿīd ibn Jubayr**: purify your heart and your intentions.
- **Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**: and beautify your character.

How can one short command mean all of that? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers from the language. **Thiyāb** is the plural of **thawb**, which in its primary sense refers to clothes or garment — but *thawb* and *libās* are at times used metaphorically for a person's **action, heart, soul, moral character and religion**, and a man's body may also be referred to as *libās*. The Qurʼān and Arabic idiom bear ample testimony to this, and the scholars of tafsīr took all these senses into account. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists the variant interpretations may not be suspected of contradiction or conflict: **they enrich the ayah's significance rather than compete over it.**

So the ayah signifies, at once: the body and clothes must be kept clean from all kinds of physical impurity; the heart and soul must be kept clean from false beliefs and adulterating thoughts, and free from base morals and moral decadence. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also derives from it that the garment must not be made or bought of unlawful money, nor made in a way the sacred law does not permit — and that it is forbidden to trail the pants or lower garment below the ankle, because this is likely to pollute the garment.

One practical point often missed: the injunction is **apparently not specific to prayer**; it applies under all conditions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Maẓharī) notes that the jurists have ruled that it is not permitted to keep the body and clothes unclean, without necessity, even outside prayer, nor to sit in an unclean place — necessity being the exception. It supports this with Allah's words, *"Surely Allah loves those who are most repenting, and loves those who keep themselves pure"* (2:222), and with a ḥadīth narration that *cleanliness is half the faith*. A Muslim, then, under all conditions, keeps body, clothes and house clean and pure — and maintains the inner cleanliness of the heart along with them.

## Ayah 5: "And keep away from ar-rujz"

**Ar-rujz** is explained by the weight of the early authorities as **the idols**. Ibn ʿAbbās said so in the report of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah — *ar-rujz are idols, so keep away from them* — and similar to this was said by **Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Qatādah, az-Zuhrī and Ibn Zayd**. Strikingly, the explanation is embedded in the ḥadīth itself: in al-Bukhārī's wording, Abū Salamah adds the note *"ar-rujz means idols."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that according to a narration of Ibn ʿAbbās the word signifies **any sin**, and notes that the letters may be read *rujz* or *rijz*, the word having the same significance either way.

Ibn Kathīr places the command alongside two parallels from the Qurʼān: *"O Prophet! Have taqwā of Allah, and obey not the disbelievers and the hypocrites"* (33:1), and Mūsā's charge to his brother Hārūn, *"Replace me among my people, act well and follow not the way of the corrupters"* (7:142). In each, a prophet is directed away from what corrupts.

But this raises an obvious question — the Prophet ﷺ never indulged in idolatry at any time in his life. Why command him? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two answers. He is commanded, **for emphasis**, to abstain from it in future as he kept away from it in the past. And the command is **in actual fact directed to the idolaters**, so that they may realise the importance of abstaining from idol-worship — since it enjoins the Prophet ﷺ to shun all filth, idols and sins, despite his being sinless and infallible.

## Ayah 6: "And give not a thing in order to have more"

**Wa lā tamnun tastakthir.** Ibn Kathīr reports Ibn ʿAbbās's reading: **do not give any gift seeking to get back in return more than it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows this, and draws out the ruling: it is reprehensible to give someone a gift with the intention that the person will give him a higher gift. Although it seems to be allowed for common people by another ayah of the Qurʼān, it remains reprehensible and morally unrighteous — and for the Prophet ﷺ especially, as Ibn ʿAbbās explained, it is unlawful.

There is a second reading in Ibn Kathīr, from **Mujāhid** (reported by Khuṣayf), which turns on the root: *"do not slacken in seeking more good — tamnun in the language of the Arabs means to become weak."* On this reading the ayah says: do not go slack in the pursuit of more good. Ibn Kathīr's rendering of the ayah also carries a third possibility in parenthesis: **consider not your deeds of obedience to Allah as a favour to Him.**

Read together, these readings guard the same nerve. A man who has just been commanded to go out and warn is being told, in the same breath, not to give in order to receive, not to count his obedience to Allah as a favour done to Him — and at the same time, not to grow weak in seeking more good.

## Ayah 7: "And be patient for the sake of your Lord"

The last of the six injunctions names the fuel for the other five.

**Ṣabr**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, literally signifies **to restrain oneself**, and in the Qurʼānic context the word has a very wide scope: to bind oneself to the laws of Allah, to restrain oneself from the things He has made unlawful, and to control oneself, as far as possible, from unnecessary bewailing and complaining in times of difficulty and hardship. So comprehensive is this injunction, the commentary says, that it **embraces almost the entire religion**.

Why patience *here*? Because of what has just been commanded. The earlier ayat directed him to invite people towards the true faith and to avoid disbelief and shirk — and it is obvious, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, that he will be opposed and persecuted by the forces of evil as a result of his missionary efforts. He should therefore be ready to bear all opposition and persecution with patience and fortitude.

And notice for whom. The ayah does not say *be patient*; it says **for your Lord, be patient**. Ibn Kathīr, citing **Mujāhid**, reads it exactly so: make your patience with their harms be **for the Face of your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic**. **Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī** said: be patient in your giving for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

## What these seven ayat ask of us

The passage moves in one clean arc: an address, then out into the world, then a fixed centre (magnify your Lord), then cleanliness of body, heart and character, then keeping away from what is false, then purity of motive, then patience for Allah's sake. The seal on it is the Prophet's ﷺ own words — after this, the revelation started coming strongly and frequently in succession. The wrapping was over.

For a believer reading it now, the shape is portable. The call came to a man wrapped in his cloak, and its first word was *arise*. What the six injunctions ask is that when you rise, you rise for Him: warning others out of love and affection rather than contempt, proclaiming His greatness with tongue and conduct, keeping garment, heart and character clean, keeping away from what is false, keeping your giving free of calculation, and bearing whatever comes back at you — *for your Lord*.

passages.title: The Trumpet and a Day of hardship
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat turn from what the Prophet ﷺ has been commanded to do to the event that gives those commands their urgency. What holds the three together is a single sentence with a hinge in it: *when* the Trumpet is sounded (ayah 8), *then* that is a hard Day (ayah 9), far from easy for the disbelievers (ayah 10).

## Where these ayat sit

Ayat 1–7 are a set of instructions to a man wrapped in his cloak: arise and warn, magnify your Lord, purify your garments, keep away from Ar-Rujz, give not a thing in order to have more, and be patient for the sake of your Lord. Ayah 8 then opens with "Then, when" — and the subject changes from the messenger's duty to the Day that duty is about. Ibn Kathir marks the shift with a heading of his own: *Reminding of the Day of Judgement.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same turn in a single sentence: "Having given these few injunctions to the Holy Prophet, the verses further refer to the Hereafter and its horrors."

Ibn Kathir cites two separate reports about the circumstances in which the opening ayat came down, and he does not combine them. One is confirmed in Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, from Jabir bin 'Abdullah, about the pause in revelation: the Prophet ﷺ heard a voice from the sky, saw the same angel who had come to him at the cave of Hira' seated on a chair between the sky and the earth, fled in fear until he fell to the ground, came to his family saying "Wrap me up, wrap me up," and Allah revealed *"O you wrapped up! Arise and warn!"* The other is recorded by At-Tabarani from Ibn 'Abbas: Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah laid on food for the Quraysh and asked them what they had to say about "this man"; they went back and forth — magician, soothsayer, poet — until they agreed to call it magic of an ancient kind; and when the news reached the Prophet ﷺ he became grieved, covered his head and wrapped himself up.

Whichever occasion is in view, the shape of the passage is the same. A man is told to stand up and speak in a hostile city — and then he is shown what he is warning them about.

## The Naqūr

**The word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it plainly: *nāqūr* means "trumpet," and the verb *nuqira* means "to blow into the trumpet so that it makes a loud high sound."

**The early commentators.** Ibn Kathir lists them one after another — Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ash-Sha'bi, Zayd bin Aslam, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd — all saying of *an-Nāqūr*: "It is the Trumpet." Mujahid adds a detail about its form: "It is in the shape of a horn."

**Notice how the ayah is phrased.** "Then, when the Naqūr is sounded" — the verb is passive. The ayah names no blower, and it gives no date. It gives us a sound, and the world on the other side of it. What ayah 8 leaves unnamed, the hadith that follows fills in.

## From the Sunnah: the horn already at the lips

Ibn Kathir brings a narration on this very ayah with its chain stated in full: Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that Abu Sa'id Al-Ashaj told them that Asbat bin Muhammad related to them from Mutarrif, from 'Atiyah Al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "How can I be comfortable when the one with the horn has placed it in his mouth, leaned his forehead forward, and is waiting to be commanded so that he can blow?"

Ibn Kathir notes that Imam Ahmad recorded it in the same way, on the authority of Asbat.

Sit with the image. The trumpet is not being fetched. It is already in the mouth. The forehead is already bent forward. The whole posture is that of someone braced for a signal, waiting on a command that has not yet been given. That is why the Prophet ﷺ asked how he could be at ease — and it is why ayah 8 says "when," not "if."

The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "What do you command us, O Messenger of Allah?" He replied:

> "Say: 'Allah is sufficient for us, and what an excellent Trustee He is. We put our trust in Allah.'"

*Ḥasbunā-llāhu wa ni'ma-l-wakīl, 'ala-llāhi tawakkalnā.* This is the answer given to those who felt the weight of what they had just heard: not calculation, not paralysis, but handing the whole matter over to the One who holds it. And notice how it sits alongside ayah 7 — "be patient for the sake of your Lord." Patience and reliance are two halves of standing steady before something you cannot control.

## "A Hard Day" — and for whom

**Ayah 9: severity, stated flatly.** *Fa-dhālika yawma'idhin yawmun 'asīr* — "that will truly be a difficult Day." Ibn Kathir's whole gloss on it is one word: **severe.** He does not decorate it. Some things are more frightening said plainly.

**Ayah 10: not easy.** *'Ala-l-kāfirīna ghayru yasīr* — "far from easy for the disbelievers." Ibn Kathir keeps to the same restraint: "meaning, it will not be easy for them."

**And note who is specified.** Ayah 9 describes the Day itself as hard; ayah 10 names *al-kāfirīn* — those who rejected the message. The Qur'an records that they themselves will say what kind of Day it is. Ibn Kathir brings the parallel: **"The disbelievers will say: 'This a Hard Day'"** (54:8).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds where the sūrah goes from here: after stating that the Day of Doom will be very horrible for all the infidels, it turns to describe one particular arrogant and conceited disbeliever — a great mischief-maker whose punishment will be as grave as the enormity of his sins. The general warning narrows to a single named case. That is worth carrying into the ayat that follow.

## A man who could not finish the ayah

Ibn Kathir closes with a report about Zurarah bin Awfa, the judge of Al-Basrah. He led the people in the morning prayer and recited this sūrah. When he reached *"Then, when the Naqūr is sounded. Truly, that Day will be a Hard Day — far from easy for the disbelievers,"* he made a moaning sound, and then he fell down dead. Ibn Kathir adds: may Allah have mercy on him.

The story is not told so that we can perform an emotion we do not have. It is told to show what these words are capable of doing to a heart that is actually listening. Most of us recite the passage and move on. He heard it.

## Living it

**Take a warning as an act of care.** The Prophet ﷺ was told to arise and warn — which Ibn Kathir explains as preparing to go forth with zeal and warn the people. Warning someone is not hostility; it is a serious form of concern. Worth remembering both when we give a reminder and when we receive one.

**Let the horn set your pace.** If the one with the horn is already braced, waiting on a word, then the case for postponing repentance collapses. There is no announced interval to plan around.

**Answer dread with the words he ﷺ gave.** When his Companions asked what to do, he did not tell them to stop thinking about it. He gave them a sentence to say: *Ḥasbunā-llāhu wa ni'ma-l-wakīl, 'ala-llāhi tawakkalnā.*

**And be patient for the sake of your Lord.** Ibn Kathir reports Mujahid's explanation of ayah 7: make your patience with their harms be for the Face of your Lord, the Mighty and Majestic — not for your reputation, not to look composed, but for Him. Ibrahim An-Nakha'i read it as patience in giving for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why patience is commanded here at all: *ṣabr* literally means "to restrain oneself," and in the Qur'an it stretches to binding oneself to the laws of Allah, restraining oneself from what He has made unlawful, and controlling, as far as possible, unnecessary bewailing and complaint in times of hardship — an injunction so comprehensive that it "embraces almost the entire religion." Having been directed to invite people to the true faith and away from disbelief and shirk, he would certainly be opposed and persecuted, and so had to be ready to bear it. The endurance this passage asks for is endurance aimed at Allah, held up by the certainty of a Day that is coming whether anyone believes in it or not.

passages.title: Wealth, sons, and a man who wanted more
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are a single unbroken stretch in which Allah counts out, item by item, everything He gave to one particular man — and turns that list of favours into the case against him. He arrived in the world with nothing; Allah gave him wealth, sons, and a life made easy; and after all of it he is still hungry for more, while calling the revelation of Allah a lie.

Ibn Kathir heads this whole section "A Threat for Whoever claims that the Qur'an is Magic," and summarises it exactly: Allah "threatens this wicked person whom He has favored with the blessings of this world, yet he is ungrateful for the blessings of Allah and he meets them with disbelief (in Allah) and rejection of His Ayat." That is the arc of ayat 11–15 in one line. The man begins **waḥīdā** — which Ibn Kathir explains as coming out of his mother's womb "alone, without any wealth or children" — and by the end of ayah 15 he is, in the words of the translation before us, "hungry for more." Everything in between is the distance Allah's generosity carried him.

## "Leave Me and the one I created" (ayah 11)

The passage opens not with the man but with a word addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: *dharnī* — the translation renders it "And leave to me ˹O Prophet˺ the one I created all by Myself." Step aside; this one is My affair. It is the language of a threat, and Ibn Kathir reads the whole passage in that key: Allah "recounts to him His favors upon him" — and the recounting is itself the indictment.

Then the description: **waḥīdā**. Ibn Kathir explains the word of the man himself: "he came out of the womb of his mother alone, without any wealth or children." Whatever he later became, he began as one bare human being who owned nothing and had brought nothing with him. That single word quietly settles the whole argument before the argument has even started: nothing on the list that follows was his by right.

## The man behind the ayat: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah

Ibn Kathir names him: "Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah Al-Makhzumi. He was one of the chiefs of the Quraysh."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scale of the man. According to Ibn ʿAbbas, his land, property and gardens stretched from Makkah to Taʼif. According to Thauri, his annual income was ten million dinars; some scholars estimated less than this amount, but Maʿārif notes it is nonetheless agreed that "the income and yearly produce of his fields and gardens were available in every season, winter or summer" — money that never had an off-season. He was, Maʿārif says, recognised as the Arab leader, known among his fellow citizens by the title *raihanah* — "the Fragrance" of the Quraysh. And citing Qurtubi, Maʿārif records how he spoke of himself: **Wahid Ibn-ul-Wahid**, "Unique, the son of the Unique" — meaning, in his own words, "Neither I have any match in my nation, nor my father Mughirah."

Hold that boast next to ayah 11. He built his name on being *the Unique One*. Allah uses the word *waḥīdā* of him too — and Ibn Kathir's explanation of it is not "peerless" but simply *alone*: a single creature Allah brought out of a womb with nothing in his hands.

## What actually happened: the visit of Abu Jahl

The sources give two tellings of the incident, and together they are the most illuminating thing in the passage.

**Ibn Kathir's account**, reported by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas: al-Walid entered the house of Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah and asked him about the Qur'an. When Abu Bakr informed him about it, al-Walid left and went to the Quraysh saying: "What a great thing this is that Ibn Abi Kabshah is saying. I swear by Allah that it is not poetry, nor magic, nor the prattling of insanity. Verily, his speech is from the Words of Allah!"

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān**, drawing on Qurtubi, records a moment of the same kind: al-Walid heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting the opening of sūrah 40 — *Ḥā Mīm. This is revelation of the Book from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing, the One who forgives sins and accepts repentance…* (40:1–3) — and exclaimed spontaneously: "By Allah! I have heard such a speech from him as can neither be the speech of a mortal, nor of Jinn. It has sweetness and elegance. Its upper part is fruit-bearing, and its lower part causes water to flow. Its beauty, no doubt, surpasses the beauty of all speeches, and cannot be superseded. It is not the speech of any human being."

Maʿārif describes what that testimony did: when the Quraysh heard what "the great wealthy Arab leader" had to say, "it created a great convulsion in the Quraish, because it resulted in a wide inclination of the people towards Islam." The chiefs gathered, alarmed, and in Ibn Kathir's wording said, "By Allah, if Al-Walid converts all of the Quraysh will convert." Abu Jahl volunteered: "By Allah, I will deal with him for you."

What Abu Jahl used as his weapon was not an argument. It was al-Walid's pride. He sat next to him pretending to be very sad, and told him the Quraysh had decided to collect money to help him in his old age — and that they were saying he only frequented the house of Abu Bakr in order to get some of his food. Maʿārif is explicit that both claims were lies, invented merely to make him angry. They worked. Al-Walid's answer, in Ibn Kathir's narration, is the sentence on which this entire passage turns:

> "Don't I have more wealth and children than they do?"

And in Maʿārif's telling, swearing by Lat and ʿUzza: "I am not in need of their food. Do they not know that I am superior to them in abundance of wealth?"

Now read ayat 12–13 with that retort still in your ears. *And I gave him extensive wealth, and sons present before his eyes.* Ibn Kathir's framing of the passage is that Allah "recounts to him His favors upon him": the wealth is what "Allah provided him with," the sons are what "Allah then made for him." The rebuttal is not that he was wrong about his fortune. It is that the very things he was holding up as his own credentials came from a Giver he never once asked about.

Maʿārif then records the rest of the conversation, which is worth knowing because of what the two men concede to each other. Al-Walid put Abu Jahl through it point by point: you say he is insane — did you ever see him perform any act of insanity? "Never, by Allah!" A soothsayer — did you hear him speak like one? No. A poet — did you hear him recite poetry? No. A liar — did you ever hear him telling a lie? Abu Jahl was forced to concede that they had never heard him tell a lie; Maʿārif reminds us that these were the very people who had conferred on him the titles *As-Sadiq*, "The Truthful," and *Al-Amin*, "The Honest." Only when every accusation had collapsed did Abu Jahl ask, "Then, you tell me what we should say about him?" — and al-Walid started thinking, raised his eyes, frowned in a hateful manner, and produced the word "magician," on the invented ground that this speech separates husband from wife, brother from brother, and father from son.

Maʿārif's verdict on him is severe and precise: "The wretched Walid was fully convinced of the veracity of the Messengership of the Holy Prophet, but his anger got the better of him, and being vanquished by his arrogance and conceit, he had decided to oppose him." He was not confused. He was cornered by his own vanity, and he chose. Ibn Kathir's comment on the man's craving for more in ayah 15 lands on exactly the same point: it "refers to his ungratefulness for his blessings **after knowing** (these blessings)."

## The inventory, item by item

The passage is built as a list of gifts, and each item is given its own weight.

**Extensive wealth (ayah 12): *mālan mamdūdā*.** Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: "vast and abundant." Maʿārif's detail makes the phrase tangible: gardens from Makkah to Taʼif, and produce available in every season, winter or summer — wealth with no lean months in it.

**Sons present before his eyes (ayah 13): *banīna shuhūdā*.** Mujahid's gloss is two words: "They are not absent." Ibn Kathir unpacks what that meant for a merchant chieftain: "They do not travel for business and trade. Rather, their servants and hired workers handle all of that for them while they are sitting with their father. He enjoys their company and delights in being with them." How many? The sources differ, and both views are preserved: As-Suddi, Abu Malik and ʿAsim bin ʿUmar bin Qatadah said they were thirteen; Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said ten. Either way, Ibn Kathir adds, "This was a great blessing in their living with him."

**A life made easy (ayah 14): *wa mahhadtu lahu tamhīdā*.** Ibn Kathir's gloss: "I made possible for him to amass wealth, luxuries and other than that." Not merely comfort — the whole apparatus by which comfort keeps arriving.

**Then he wants more (ayah 15): *thumma yaṭmaʿu an azīd*.** The translation before us reads it "Yet he is hungry for more," and Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps the sequence in view: "After all that he desires that I should give more." *After all that* — you can hear the sheer nerve of it. And notice who is speaking throughout: *I created … I gave him … I made life easy for him … that I should give more.* Four first-person acts of Allah, and one man in the middle of them who thought the whole story was about himself.

## Living it

**Every blessing is a loan with a name on it.** The argument of this passage does not require you to be rich, only to be forgetful. Ayah 11 is the antidote: Ibn Kathir's picture of a man coming out of the womb alone, without any wealth or children, is a picture of every one of us. Whatever is in your hands now arrived from somewhere. Gratitude is simply keeping that fact in view — and ayah 15 shows what happens when it slips: not contentment, but hunger for more.

**Children beside you are part of the gift.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a striking lesson out of *banīna shuhūdā* — and it is easy to skim past that this appears in a list of *favours*. "Just as the birth of children and their being alive are a boon of Allah, their staying with parents is also a great divine blessing, because it is the cause of coolness of their eyes and a satisfaction of their heart," and because children who are present can be of assistance to their parents. Maʿārif then turns to our own age: parents who send their children off to foreign countries and are happy at their staying overseas for years, not minding whether they see their faces at all so long as reports of huge earnings keep arriving — this, Maʿārif says, "indicates that they are unaware of the concept of peace and comfort," and he traces it to forgetting Allah, quoting *those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget their own selves* (59:19). Presence is a blessing that money is very good at persuading us to sell.

**The real danger in this passage is not ignorance — it is knowing and not bowing.** Al-Walid heard the Qur'an, tested it against poetry, soothsaying and madness, and called it the Word of Allah. What defeated him was a jibe about charity and a rumour about a meal. Maʿārif observes that the unbelievers of that age, for all their sins, "abstained from the enormity of telling lies" for fear of being socially stigmatised as liars — which is why al-Walid had to labour to construct the word "magician" rather than simply lie outright — and then adds with sorrow that in our own time "telling lies is no sin. It is in fact treated as a great art. Let alone unbelievers, even the pious and religious Muslims do not find it hateful… We seek Allah's refuge from such an attitude."

So ask, when truth arrives and something in you resists it: is this an objection, or is it a wound? Al-Walid's answer to that question cost him everything Allah had spent five ayat listing.

passages.title: Obstinate to Our signs: how he plotted
passages.tafsir:
Ayat 16–20 pass sentence on a man in Makkah who heard the Qur'an, and then sat down and worked out what to call it. The commentators identify him, and the ayat themselves lay out the case against him in five short steps.

The passage moves as one argument: a verdict (16, "he has been truly stubborn with Our revelations"), a sentence (17, "I will make his fate unbearable"), the crime that earned it (18, "for he contemplated and determined…"), and then the curse pronounced on that crime, twice over (19–20, "May he be condemned! How evil was what he determined!"). Notice what is finally condemned in 19 and 20. Not his wealth, and not simply that he disbelieved, but — in the words of the ayat themselves — *how he determined*.

## The man named in the commentaries

Ibn Kathir names him: Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah Al-Makhzumi, "one of the chiefs of the Quraysh — may Allah curse him."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scale of his life. According to Ibn ʿAbbas, his land, property and gardens stretched from Makkah to Taʼif. According to Thauri, his annual income was ten million dinars; some scholars estimated less than this, but it is agreed that the produce of his fields and gardens came in every season, winter or summer. He was known among his fellow citizens by the title *raihanah* — "the Fragrance" — of the Quraysh, and he used to refer to himself boastfully as "Unique, the son of the Unique," meaning, as Maʿārif explains it, "Neither I have any match in my nation, nor my father Mughirah." Maʿārif attributes this to Qurtubi.

Ibn Kathir sets that wealth against where the man started. Commenting on the ayah "Leave Me alone (to deal) with whom I created lonely," he explains: "he came out of the womb of his mother alone, without any wealth or children." The children came later — thirteen in number according to As-Suddi, Abu Malik and ʿAsim bin ʿUmar bin Qatadah; ten according to Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. All of it was given to a man who had arrived with nothing.

That is the background the passage rests on. Ayat 16–20 are about what he did with it.

## Ayah 16 — "But no!"

**كَلَّا ۖ إِنَّهُ كَانَ لِآيَاتِنَا عَنِيدًا**
*"But no! ˹For˺ he has been truly stubborn with Our revelations."*

Ibn Kathir renders the same words, "Nay! Verily, he has been opposing Our Ayat," and he quotes them joined to the ayah immediately before: "(After all that he desires that I should give more. Nay! Verily, he has been opposing Our Ayat.)" The refusal lands directly on the appetite for more. He wanted the account extended; the account is closed instead.

Then Ibn Kathir gives the verdict in a single word — "meaning, obstinate" — and follows it with the sentence that unlocks the whole passage:

> "This refers to his ungratefulness for his blessings **after knowing** (these blessings)."

Hold those two together: *obstinate*, and *ungrateful after knowing*. On Ibn Kathir's reading the charge is not that he failed to see. It is that he saw, and dug in. And note what he set himself against. Ibn Kathir's summary of the man is that he "meets them with disbelief (in Allah) and rejection of His Ayat" — the *āyāt*, the revelations and signs Allah Himself sent down.

## Ayah 17 — "I will make his fate unbearable"

**سَأُرْهِقُهُ صَعُودًا**
*"I will make his fate unbearable"* — or, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "I shall force him to Sa'ud."

Ibn Kathir reports four sayings of the early authorities about *Sa'ud*, and sets them side by side without choosing between them:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas**, reported by Qatadah: "Sa'ud is a rock in Hell that the disbeliever will be dragged across on his face."
- **As-Suddi**: "Sa'ud is a slippery rock in Hell that he will be forced to climb."
- **Mujahid**: "This is a harsh portion of the torment."
- **Qatadah**: "It is a torment that contains no relaxation (break for relief)."

Two of these describe a place; two describe the severity. Qatadah's is the one that lingers — a torment with no break for relief in it.

Ibn Kathir then ties this sentence to the crime named in the next ayah. Commenting on "Verily, he thought and plotted," he writes: "We only caused him to face the grievous torment of Sa'ud, that is Our bringing him close to the harsh torment, because he was far away from faith. This was because he thought and plotted." The translation before you carries the same link in its opening word — *"**for** he contemplated and determined."* Ayah 17 is the sentence; ayah 18 is the reason.

## Ayah 18 — "he contemplated and determined"

**إِنَّهُ فَكَّرَ وَقَدَّرَ**

Both verbs are verbs of the mind at work, and the two commentaries render them slightly differently. Ibn Kathir has "he thought and plotted," and glosses the second verb: "*and plotted*, meaning, he contemplated." Maʿārif renders the ayah "He pondered and suggested," and notes that "the word *qaddara* is derived from *taqdir*, and literally denotes 'to suggest.'" Between the two, the picture is of deliberation — a man weighing what to put forward.

Ibn Kathir says exactly what he was deliberating about:

> "he contemplated what he should say about the Qur'an when he was asked about it. So he deliberated over what statement he should invent against it."

Hold on to that. On this reading the charge in these ayat is not that he misunderstood the Qur'an. It is that he went looking for a serviceable thing to say against it.

## What the reports say about it

The commentaries preserve more than one narration here, and they are not the same story told twice. They differ in setting, in cast, and in what they report him saying. It is worth reading them as they come, separately.

**Ibn Kathir, reporting from Al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.** Al-Walid went into the house of Abu Bakr bin Abi Quhafah and asked him about the Qur'an. When Abu Bakr told him about it, he left, went to the Quraysh and said: "What a great thing this is that Ibn Abi Kabshah is saying. I swear by Allah that it is not poetry, nor magic, nor the prattling of insanity. Verily, his speech is from the Words of Allah!"

The Quraysh understood what that meant. They gathered and said, "By Allah, if Al-Walid converts (to Islam) all of the Quraysh will convert." Abu Jahl bin Hisham said, "By Allah, I will deal with him for you." He went to Al-Walid's house and asked, "Don't you see that your people are collecting charity for you?" Al-Walid bristled: "Don't I have more wealth and children than they do?" Abu Jahl pressed further: "They are saying that you only went to Ibn Abi Quhafah's house so that you can get some of his food." That was enough. Al-Walid answered: "Is this what my tribe is saying? Nay, by Allah, I am not seeking to be close to Ibn Abi Quhafah, nor ʿUmar, nor Ibn Abi Kabshah. And his speech is only inherited magic of old."

Ibn Kathir adds that Allah then revealed to His Messenger ﷺ the passage running from "Leave me alone with whom I created lonely" down to "It spares not, nor does it leave (anything)!" — a stretch of revelation wider than the five ayat we are reading, with ours sitting inside it.

**Qatadah's report, also in Ibn Kathir.** Ibn Kathir gives it with its own hedge: Qatadah said, "*They claim* that he (Al-Walid) said, 'By Allah, I thought about what the man says, and it is not poetry. Verily, it has a sweetness and it is truly elegant. Verily, it is exalted and it is not overcome. And I have no doubt that it is magic.'" Qatadah adds that Allah then revealed "So let him be cursed, how he plotted!" — ayah 19 itself. Read the quotation slowly: every clause is praise, until the last one, which turns the praise into an accusation.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, recounting the story from Qurtubi.** This is a different account with much more in it. Al-Walid heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting the opening of the fortieth sūrah — "Ha Meem. This is revelation of the Book from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing, the One who forgives sins and accepts repentance, the One who is severe in punishment…" (40:1–3) — and, in Maʿārif's words, "exclaimed spontaneously, in which he was forced to concede": "By Allah! I have heard such a speech from him as can neither be the speech of a mortal, nor of Jinn. It has sweetness and elegance. Its upper part is fruit-bearing, and its lower part causes water to flow. Its beauty, no doubt, surpasses the beauty of all speeches, and cannot be superseded. It is not the speech of any human being."

When the Quraysh heard what their great wealthy leader had said, "it created a great convulsion" among them, because people began inclining towards Islam in numbers. Abu Jahl took on the job of fixing it. He came and sat beside Al-Walid pretending to be very sad, and when asked what was wrong, told him the Quraysh had decided to collect money to help him in his old age — because they had learnt that he visits Muhammad ﷺ and the son of Abu Quhafah for the sake of a meal, and flatters and praises their speech to that end. Maʿārif states plainly that both halves of this were lies, "invented merely to make him angry." It worked. He swore by Lat and ʿUzza that he had no need of their food, and demanded: "Do they not know that I am superior to them in abundance of wealth?"

Then — and this is the striking part of this account — Al-Walid took the charges against the Prophet ﷺ apart one at a time. *You say Muhammad is insane: did you ever see him perform any act of insanity?* Abu Jahl: "Never, by Allah!" *You claim he is a soothsayer: did you hear him speak like a soothsayer? We know well the utterings of the soothsayers.* Abu Jahl had to admit, "No, by Allah!" *You say he is a poet: did you hear him recite poetry?* He had not. *You say he is a liar: did you ever hear him telling a lie?* "Abu Jahl was forced to concede that they had never heard him tell a lie" — and Maʿārif adds the detail that these same people "had conferred upon him the titles of As-Sadiq 'The Truthful' and Al-ʿAmin 'The Honest.'"

Every charge collapsed. Abu Jahl was left with the only question he had: "Then, you tell me what we should say about him?"

"Walid started thinking, then he raised his eyes towards Abu Jahl, frowned in a hateful manner, and ultimately replied, 'I think he is certainly a magician.'" Maʿārif notes at once: "He knew well that the Holy Prophet is not a magician either." So he supplied a reason for the label — "Do you not see how his speech separates husband from wife, brother from brother and father from son? This is the magical effect of faith. As soon as a person embraces the faith, he begins to hate his unbelieving mother, father and other relatives."

Maʿārif's summary of the man is severe and exact:

> "The wretched Walid was fully convinced of the veracity of the Messengership of the Holy Prophet, but his anger got the better of him, and being vanquished by his arrogance and conceit, he had decided to oppose him. However, he wanted to abstain from lying openly, so that he might not be exposed to shame and disgrace. Therefore, he pondered very carefully, and suggested that he should be labelled a 'magician'."

That paragraph is a commentary on ayah 18. He pondered, and he suggested.

## Ayat 19–20 — condemned, and condemned again

**فَقُتِلَ كَيْفَ قَدَّرَ ۝ ثُمَّ قُتِلَ كَيْفَ قَدَّرَ**
*"May he be condemned! How evil was what he determined! May he be condemned even more! How evil was what he determined!"*

The renderings differ in force. Ibn Kathir has "So let him be cursed, how he plotted! And once more let him be cursed, how he plotted!" Maʿārif has "Death onto him! How [bad] is the suggestion he has put forward! Again, death unto him!" Ibn Kathir's note on the pair is a single line: **"This is a supplication against him."**

Two things in these two ayat deserve attention.

**First, what is condemned.** Not how rich he was, not even, in so many words, that he disbelieved — but *kayfa qaddara*, how he determined, how he put his suggestion forward. The ayat fix on the deliberating itself: the weighing, the search for a workable label. This is the same deliberating that Ibn Kathir described as "he deliberated over what statement he should invent against it," and that Maʿārif described as pondering "very carefully" in order to arrive at "magician." That is what the curse falls on.

**Second, the repetition.** The condemnation is not said once. Ayah 20 says it again, and Maʿārif notes exactly this in its comment on the passage: "He is therefore cursed repeatedly in the verses cited above." The reader is meant to hear it land, and then land a second time.

## Living with these ayat

**Knowledge raises the stakes; it does not lower them.** Ibn Kathir's phrase is the sharpest warning in the passage: ungrateful for his blessings *after knowing* them. Maʿārif says the same thing from the other side — he was "fully convinced of the veracity of the Messengership of the Holy Prophet." His problem was never a shortage of information. Anyone who sits and reads tafsir is being handed, in his own small measure, a share of that same clarity. What is done with it is the whole question.

**Watch what the reports say actually moved him.** In both the Al-ʿAwfi narration and the account Maʿārif takes from Qurtubi, the turn does not come from an argument about the Qur'an. It comes from a jab at his standing — the suggestion that his people thought him a charity case, taking meals off Abu Bakr's table. Maʿārif names the mechanism outright: "his anger got the better of him, and being vanquished by his arrogance and conceit, he had decided to oppose him." Reputation is a heavier idol than most of us will admit.

**A note Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out, and turns on us.** Al-Walid wanted to oppose the Prophet ﷺ but "wanted to abstain from lying openly, so that he might not be exposed to shame and disgrace." Maʿārif reflects that the unbelievers of that age were involved in every kind of sin, yet "abstained from the enormity of telling lies" — pointing to Abu Sufyan's statement in the court of Heraclius, where the pagans were willing to sacrifice their lives and children in opposing the Prophet ﷺ, but not willing to lie and be socially stigmatised as liars. Then the book turns the point on our own time: today lying "is in fact treated as a great art. Let alone unbelievers, even the pious and religious Muslims do not find it hateful… We seek Allah's refuge from such an attitude."

**And gratitude is itself a form of honesty.** The ayat just before this passage are a list of gifts; ayah 16 is what the recipient did with them. Maʿārif dwells on one of those gifts in particular — that children not merely being born and alive, but *staying* with their parents, is "a great divine blessing, because it is the cause of coolness of their eyes and a satisfaction of their heart." Every blessing listed there is one most of us hold in some measure. To receive all of it and then meet Allah's revelations with the obstinacy of ayah 16 is the posture these five ayat exist to warn us out of.

passages.title: This is only magic - and the sentence of Saqar
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are a slow-motion portrait of one man's face in the moment he decided what to say about the Qur'an. Allah has just recounted the blessings He poured on him and warned of the torment awaiting him; now He replays the scene gesture by gesture — *then* he thought, *then* he frowned, *then* he scowled, *then* he turned his back — until the verdict leaves his mouth in ayat 24–25 and Allah pronounces His own sentence in ayah 26. What holds the passage together is that chain of "then… then… then…", and the fact that a man's private calculation is being read back to him aloud.

## The man behind the pronoun

Ibn Kathir names him: **Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah Al-Makhzumi**, one of the chiefs of the Quraysh. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scale of his life: on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, his land, property and gardens stretched from Makkah to Taʼif; Thauri put his annual income at ten million dinars, though some scholars have estimated less than that amount. What is agreed, says the commentary, is that the income and yearly produce of his fields and gardens were available in every season, winter or summer — an income that never paused. He was recognised as the Arab leader, known among his fellow citizens by the title *raihanah* — "the Fragrance" — of the Quraysh, and he used to refer to himself boastfully as *Wahid Ibn-ul-Wahid*, "Unique, the son of the Unique," meaning that neither he nor his father Mughirah had any match (Qurtubi, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

That is the man Ibn Kathir describes as one "whom He has favored with the blessings of this world, yet he is ungrateful for the blessings of Allah and he meets them with disbelief (in Allah) and rejection of His Ayat. He invents lies against Allah's Ayat and claims that they are the words of a man."

## What he actually said about the Qur'an

The most striking thing in the sources is that Al-Walid never claimed the Qur'an was ordinary. He said the opposite — twice, and in public.

**The first testimony.** Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas (in Ibn Kathir) that Al-Walid entered the house of Abu Bakr bin Abi Quhafah and asked him about the Qur'an. When Abu Bakr informed him about it, he left and went to the Quraysh saying: "What a great thing this is… I swear by Allah that it is not poetry, nor magic, nor the prattling of insanity. Verily, his speech is from the Words of Allah!"

The Quraysh understood exactly what that meant. A group of them gathered and said: "By Allah, if Al-Walid converts (to Islam) all of the Quraysh will convert." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that his words created a great convulsion among the Quraysh, because they resulted in a wide inclination of the people towards Islam. Their whole social order was one man's sentence away from turning over.

**The second testimony.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, following Qurtubi, records that Al-Walid heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting the passage at 40:1–3 — *Ḥā Mīm. This is revelation of the Book from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing, the One who forgives sins and accepts repentance…* — and the words escaped him spontaneously:

> "By Allah! I have heard such a speech from him [Muhammad] as can neither be the speech of a mortal, nor of Jinn. It has sweetness and elegance. Its upper part is fruit-bearing, and its lower part causes water to flow. Its beauty, no doubt, surpasses the beauty of all speeches, and cannot be superseded. It is not the speech of any human being."

That is not politeness. That is a man reaching for the image of a well-watered fruit tree because the ordinary vocabulary of criticism had run out on him. Qatadah's report in Ibn Kathir preserves the same admission with the poison already stirred in: "By Allah, I thought about what the man says, and it is not poetry. Verily, it has a sweetness and it is truly elegant. Verily, it is exalted and it is not overcome. And I have no doubt that it is magic."

Hold on to that last sentence. Everything true comes first; the verdict contradicts all of it.

## The visit that changed his mouth

When Abu Jahl bin Hisham heard the Quraysh panicking he said, "By Allah, I will deal with him for you," and went to Al-Walid's house. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again from Qurtubi, gives the conversation at length, and it is worth following, because ayat 21–23 are a description of Al-Walid's face during it.

Abu Jahl sat down next to him, pretending to be very sad. When Al-Walid asked what was the matter, he said the Quraysh had decided to collect money for him and help him in his old age — and had now learnt that he was visiting Muhammad ﷺ and the son of Abu Quhafah in order to get some eatables from them, flattering them and praising their speech. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out plainly that both halves were untrue: it was a lie that the Quraysh were collecting money, "invented merely to make him angry," and a lie that he was getting food from the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir's version carries the same taunt — "Don't you see that your people are collecting charity for you?" — and Al-Walid's stung reply: "Don't I have more wealth and children than they do?"

Notice what the lever was. Abu Jahl did not bring a single argument against the Qur'an. He attacked the old man's standing — made him feel pitied, dependent, small in front of his people.

It worked. Al-Walid swore by Lāt and ʿUzzā — the two Arabian idols — that he was not in need of their food, and then, remarkably, began cross-examining Abu Jahl on the very slanders the Quraysh had been circulating:

- "when you say that Muhammad is insane, nobody would believe it. Did you ever see him perform any act of insanity?" — Abu Jahl answered with an oath that he never had.
- "You claim that Muhammad is a soothsayer. Did you hear him speak like a soothsayer?" — his reply was again in the negative.
- "You say that he is a poet. Did you hear him recite poetry?" — he declared that he had not.
- "You say that he is a liar. Did you ever [hear] him telling a lie?" — Abu Jahl was forced to concede that they had never heard him tell a lie.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail that gives this its weight: these were the same people who had themselves conferred upon him the titles **As-Sadiq**, "The Truthful," and **Al-Amin**, "The Honest." Al-Walid pressed further on soothsaying — "We know well the utterings of the soothsayers. Muhammad's discourse cannot be held as the utterance of a soothsayer" — and Abu Jahl again had to admit it, under oath.

Every accusation had now been withdrawn by the chief accusers themselves. So Abu Jahl put the real question: "Then, you tell me what we should say about him?"

## Ayat 21–23: the face, frame by frame

Here the Qur'an takes over the narration.

**Ayah 21 — *thumma naẓara*, "Then he re-contemplated."** The commentators read this in two complementary ways. Ibn Kathir glosses it: "he thought again and deliberated" — a second round of calculation on top of the *fakkara wa qaddara* ("he thought and plotted") that Allah has just reported of him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "Then he looked [to those around him]," which fits the Qurtubi narrative exactly: Al-Walid "started thinking, then he raised his eyes towards Abu Jahl." Whether the eyes turn inward or outward, the picture is the same — a man buying time before saying something he does not believe.

On the word *qaddara*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it derives from *taqdir* and literally denotes "to suggest" — to propose a formulation. Ibn Kathir explains that he "contemplated what he should say about the Qur'an when he was asked about it. So he deliberated over what statement he should invent against it." He was not weighing whether the Qur'an was true. He was drafting a line.

And between the first round of thought and this second one stand the two curses that Allah pronounces mid-scene — *fa-qutila kayfa qaddar, thumma qutila kayfa qaddar*. Ibn Kathir says simply: "This is a supplication against him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, "Death onto him! How [bad] is the suggestion he has put forward!" The repetition matters: sentence is passed on him mid-thought, before the words are even out of his mouth.

**Ayah 22 — *thumma ʿabasa wa basara*, "then frowned and scowled."** Two verbs for one face. On *ʿabasa*, Ibn Kathir says he "contracted his eyebrows together and frowned"; Qatadah's wording is that "He contracted his eyes together and scowled." On *basara*, Ibn Kathir says "he scowled and was disgusted." The first word photographs the muscles; the second names the sourness behind them. Qurtubi's narrative catches the same instant — he "frowned in a hateful manner" before answering. This is a man visibly at war with what he knows.

**Ayah 23 — *thumma adbara wastakbara*, "then turned his back and acted arrogantly."** Ibn Kathir: "he turned away from the truth and arrogantly refused to accept and submit to the Qur'an." The back turns outward; the self swells inward. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary of the whole episode is unsparing: "The wretched Walid was fully convinced of the veracity of the Messengership of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, but his anger got the better of him, and being vanquished by his arrogance and conceit, he had decided to oppose him."

## Ayat 24–25: the verdict he manufactured

"**This is nothing but magic from that of old**" — and Ibn Kathir unpacks what the accusation was designed to do: "this is magic that Muhammad received from those who were before him, and he is merely saying what he got from them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "traditional magic." The charge is deflating twice over: not only sorcery, but *second-hand* sorcery — nothing new, nothing from above.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves the reasoning he attached to it, because he needed a charge with an argument behind it. The passage runs: "in order to devise an excuse for saying so, he argued, 'Do you not see how his speech separates husband from wife, brother from brother and father from son? This is the magical effect of faith. As soon as a person embraces the faith, he begins to hate his unbelieving mother, father and other relatives.'"

Read it slowly and the excuse gives itself away. What is being described there is not sorcery at all — it is exactly what faith does when it enters a household and reorders a person's deepest loyalties. The truest sign of the message's power had been picked up and relabelled.

**Ayah 25 — "This is nothing but the word of a human being!"** Ibn Kathir gives the plain meaning: "it is not the Words of Allah." That is the real target of the whole exercise, and it is why Ibn Kathir titles this section "A Threat for Whoever claims that the Qur'an is Magic." Set ayah 25 beside his own earlier exclamation — "It is not the speech of any human being" — and the reversal is complete. The same Arabic word, *bashar* (a human being, a mortal), stands in both: in his private confession it denied that any mortal could have produced this speech; in his public verdict it reduces the speech to a mortal's words.

## Ayah 26: the answer that is not an argument

*Sa-uṣlīhi Saqar* — rendered here, "Soon I will burn him in Hell!"

Notice that Allah offers no rebuttal. The claim of ayat 24–25 is not debated, weighed or refuted; it is answered with a sentence. The case had already been settled in the accuser's own mouth.

Ibn Kathir explains the verb: "I will engulf him in it from all his sides." The man who *turned his back* in ayah 23 will be a man with no side left to turn to.

And Ibn Kathir draws the line of cause plainly. Earlier in the sūrah Allah had said, *saʾurhiquhu ṣaʿūdā* — "I shall force him to Saʿūd," a torment the early authorities described in differing terms (Qatadah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is "a rock in Hell that the disbeliever will be dragged across on his face"; As-Suddi, "a slippery rock in Hell that he will be forced to climb"; Mujahid, "a harsh portion of the torment"; Qatadah, "a torment that contains no relaxation"). Ibn Kathir ties that threat to this thinking: Allah brought him close to the harsh torment "because he was far away from faith… because he thought and plotted." The punishment answers the deliberation, not merely the sentence he finally spoke.

## What this passage asks of a believer

**Knowing is not submitting.** Al-Walid's problem was never a shortage of evidence. He had heard the Qur'an, judged it superior to all human and jinn speech, and said so out loud. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says he was *fully convinced*. What defeated him was anger, arrogance and conceit — and that is the warning in these ayat: a heart can be persuaded and still refuse.

**Watch what actually moves you.** Abu Jahl brought no proof. He brought humiliation — an invented story about charity and free meals, made up, as the commentary says, "merely to make him angry." The thought of being pitied by his tribe did what no argument could. It is worth asking honestly what plays that role in our own lives: whose opinion could make us say, in public, the opposite of what we know to be true.

**The lie he would not tell, and the lie he did.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a strange restraint in these people: the unbelievers and transgressors were involved in every kind of sin and shameful deed, "but they abstained from the enormity of telling lies," and it cites Abu Sufyan's statement in the royal court of Heraclius — pagans willing to sacrifice their lives and children in opposing the Prophet ﷺ, yet unwilling to be socially stigmatised as liars. Al-Walid himself, the commentary notes, "wanted to abstain from lying openly, so that he might not be exposed to shame and disgrace," which is precisely why he engineered a charge with an argument attached to it. And yet, having taken such care over the small lie, he told the largest one there is: that the speech of Allah is the word of a man. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns this on the reader's own age, where lying "is in fact treated as a great art," and where "even the pious and religious Muslims do not find it hateful" — "We seek Allah's refuge from such an attitude."

**Gratitude is the hinge.** Ibn Kathir's frame for this whole section is a man showered with wealth, with sons present at his side and a life "made smooth and comfortable," who then "desires that I should give more" and turns *ʿanīd* — obstinate — against the Ayat of the One who gave it all. Ayat 21–26 are what ingratitude looks like when it is finally forced to speak: it thinks, it hesitates, it scowls, it turns away — and then it calls the truth magic.

passages.title: Saqar and the trial of its nineteen wardens
passages.tafsir:
**Ayah 26 had just passed sentence on one man — "I will cast him into Saqar." Ayat 27–31 stop everything to answer the question that sentence leaves hanging: what is Saqar?** What holds these five ayat together is that the answer is both given and withheld. Allah names the Fire, says what it does to a body, states the number of its keepers — and then explains that even that number was released as a test, and that the full armies of the Lord are known to Him alone.

## Who the sentence was passed on

Ibn Kathir identifies the man of the preceding ayat as al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi, one of the chiefs of Quraysh. He reports from Al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas that al-Walid went into Abu Bakr's house, asked him about the Qur'an, and came away telling Quraysh that what they were hearing was neither poetry, nor magic, nor the prattling of insanity — "his speech is from the Words of Allah." Quraysh gathered in alarm: if al-Walid accepts, all of Quraysh will accept. Abu Jahl volunteered — "By Allah, I will deal with him for you" — and he did not argue religion at all. He went to al-Walid's house and told him his people were collecting charity for him, and that they were saying he only visited the house of Ibn Abi Quhafah — Abu Bakr — to get some of his food. Al-Walid answered as a proud man does: do I not have more wealth and children than they do? And then, enraged, he produced the verdict Quraysh wanted: "his speech is only inherited magic of old."

That is the deliberation ayat 18–24 replay in slow motion — he thought, he weighed, he frowned, he scowled, he turned his back and grew proud. Ibn Kathir notes that the twice-repeated "let him be cursed" is a supplication against him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail that makes the episode cold: al-Walid was fully convinced of the truth of the Prophet's ﷺ messengership, but his anger got the better of him and he was vanquished by arrogance and conceit; because he did not want to lie openly and be exposed to shame, he settled on "magician" — arguing that this speech separates husband from wife, brother from brother, father from son, as sorcery does. Ayah 26 is the verdict: *I will cast him into Saqar* — which Ibn Kathir glosses, "I will engulf him in it from all his sides."

With that, the man drops out of view and the Fire fills the frame.

## "And what will make you realize what Saqar is?" (27)

Ibn Kathir's comment on this question is brief and exact: it is said "to give fright and emphasis to its matter." Then, he continues, "Allah explains this by His saying" — and the explanation follows in the next ayat.

That is the shape of the passage. A question is put to the Prophet ﷺ, and the answer is not left to anyone's imagination; Allah supplies it Himself. There is a quiet irony in where this falls. The man's considered verdict had just been that this is "nothing but the word of a human being" — which Ibn Kathir glosses, "meaning, it is not the Words of Allah." What immediately follows is Allah describing Saqar.

## "It leaves nothing and it spares nothing" (28)

Two verbs, close in meaning, negated one after the other. The doubling leaves no remainder and no exception.

Ibn Kathir transmits what this describes: it eats their flesh, their veins, their nerves and their skins; then their organs will be changed into something else. "They will remain in this (form), not living or dying." This was stated by Ibn Buraydah, Abu Sinan and others.

Hence the rendering "It does not let anyone live or die." The two exits this world always leaves open — recovery, or an end — are both closed. The state does not resolve.

## "Scorching the skin" (29)

*Lawwāḥatun lil-bashar* — "Scorching for the humans." Ibn Kathir gathers the glosses of that last word: Mujahid said, "This means for the skin"; Qatadah, "This means burning the skin"; Ibn ʿAbbas, "Burning the skin of man."

A reader may notice something in passing. *Al-bashar* is the same word al-Walid used when he called the Qur'an "the word of *al-bashar*", a mortal's speech; it is the word here for the human surface the Fire is set against; and it is the word that closes ayah 31, "a reminder to *al-bashar*", to mankind. The commentators quoted in these pages do not draw a line between the three occurrences — the recurrence is simply there in the text for whoever reads slowly.

## "Over it are nineteen" (30)

The number is given flat, with no explanation of why nineteen. Ibn Kathir's gloss is short: these are "the first of the guardians of Hell. They are magnificent in (their appearance) and harsh in their character."

*The first of the guardians* — so ayah 30 is not a headcount of the angels of Hell. It says nineteen stand *over* it. The passage itself will guard against the misreading before it closes.

## "None but angels" (31)

Ibn Kathir records how Quraysh received the number. Abu Jahl said: "O people of Quraysh! Are not every ten among you able to defeat one of them?" Ibn Kathir then reports, with the words "It has been said", that Abu Al-Ashaddayn — his name was Kaladah bin Usayd bin Khalaf — said, "O people of Quraysh! You defend me against two of them and I will defend you against seventeen of them." He said this, Ibn Kathir notes, thinking himself to be very great; they claimed he had reached such strength that he would stand on a cow hide and ten men would try to pull it out from under his feet, and the hide would be torn to pieces and still not be removed from under him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a report in the same vein: Baihaqi transmits a narrative from Suddi that when ayah 30 was revealed, a foolish Quraysh unbeliever named Abul-Asalain spoke out, "O nation of Quraish, I alone am sufficient for the nineteen. I will take care of ten with my right arm, and nine with my left arm. Thus I will put an end to all nineteen of them."

The opening of ayah 31 answers all of it: **We have set none as guardians of the Fire but angels.** Ibn Kathir draws out the force of it — guardian angels, stern and severe, "extremely strong in their creation. They cannot be stood against nor defeated." He states plainly that the wording is a refutation of the idolaters of Quraysh when they mentioned the number of guardian angels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the reply more bluntly still: first of all, one angel is sufficient for all of them.

The mistake was not really in the arithmetic. It was in the category. These men heard a number and immediately treated the keepers of Hell as a rival clan to be out-muscled, because muscle and numbers were how they had always settled things. That is the reflex the ayah exposes: measuring the unseen with the tools of the seen.

## "Only as a trial" (31)

Then comes the sentence that lifts this passage above description: **We have fixed their number only as a trial — a *fitnah*, a test — for the disbelievers.** Ibn Kathir: "We only have mentioned their number as being nineteen as a test from Us for mankind."

Notice what is called a test. Not the Fire — the *number*. A single detail, easy to repeat, impossible to verify, and Allah released it knowing exactly how it would sort its hearers. The ayah then names that sorting:

- **The People of the Scripture arrive at certainty** — Ibn Kathir: so that they may know that this Messenger is true, "for he speaks according to the same thing that they have with them of heavenly revealed Scriptures that came to the Prophets before him."
- **The believers increase in faith** — Ibn Kathir: "This is due to what they witness from the truthfulness of the information of their Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ."
- **No doubt is left** for either group.
- **Those in whose hearts is a disease** — "among the hypocrites," says Ibn Kathir — **and the disbelievers say: "What does Allah intend by this example?"** That is, in Ibn Kathir's words: "What is the wisdom in mentioning this here?"

One sentence, four different hearts. Nothing changed but the hearer. And the ayah states the principle without softening it: *Thus Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.* Ibn Kathir comments that by way of examples like this, faith becomes firm in the hearts of some people and is shaken with others — and he adds at once that this is not arbitrary: "This has a profound wisdom and it is an irrefutable proof."

There is a warning here for anyone who reads revelation hunting for the odd detail to trip over. The detail was placed deliberately. What a person does when he meets something in the Book that he cannot weigh or measure *is* the examination.

## "And none can know the hosts of your Lord but He"

Ibn Kathir explains why this clause comes exactly here: none knows their number and their count except Allah — "This is so that one does not make the mistake of thinking that they are only nineteen in all." The number was given about those set over the Fire; it was never a census of Allah's angels.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the verse in the same direction: the number nineteen refers to the chiefs of the angels, and under each of these angels the angels of Allah are a legion beyond human count or computation — Allah alone knows their number, and they stand ready to carry out the punishment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites Muqatil, among the leading authorities, who says this clause is a rebuttal to a statement of Abu Jahl. On hearing the ayah that there are nineteen angels in charge of Hell, Abu Jahl addressed the youth of Quraysh and said that Muhammad has only nineteen companions, so there is nothing to worry about. He was matching one number against another and mocking the smallness of the Muslims. The clause does not answer him with a headcount of the believers. It tells him that the hosts of his Lord are known to Allah alone — that the ledger he was doing his sums in was never the real one.

To convey that scale, Ibn Kathir cites the hadith concerning Al-Isra' — the Night Journey — which he says is reported in the Two Sahihs and other collections, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the Frequented House, Al-Bayt Al-Maʿmur, in the seventh heaven: "Seventy thousand angels enter into it every day and they do not return to it," one visit being all that is due upon them.

Seventy thousand a day, none of them ever coming back, at a single house in the seventh heaven. That is the arithmetic Abu Jahl was proposing to do.

Then the passage lands: **And this is nothing but a reminder to mankind.** Mujahid and others said "this" refers to the Hellfire which has been described. The whole terrible description was never given to satisfy curiosity about the next world. It was given as *dhikrā* — a reminder, meant to change what a person does today.

## Living it

**Knowing is not believing.** Al-Walid's tragedy, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly, is that he was fully convinced of the truth and still opposed it — his anger got the better of him, arrogance and conceit had already decided him, and he would not risk the shame of being caught in an open lie. A person can be certain of the truth and still be lost by refusing to bow to it.

**Notice what was used to buy him.** Abu Jahl refuted nothing. He simply touched al-Walid's standing and his wealth — and al-Walid's own answer gave him away: do I not have more wealth and children than they do? The blessings Ibn Kathir lists at the head of this passage, and for which he says the man was ungrateful, became the leash. Whatever a person cannot bear to be thought less of in is the price at which his tongue can be bought.

**Do not do arithmetic with the unseen.** The nineteen are a report to be believed, not a puzzle to be solved or a force to be sized up. Ibn Kathir's guidance on the closing clause is the posture the passage asks for: their number is known to Allah alone, and nineteen is what stands over the Fire, not the sum of His hosts. We affirm the Fire, its wardens and their number exactly as Allah has told us, without adding to it and without explaining it away.

**Let the reminder do its work.** These ayat describe a fire that consumes without ever finishing and a guard that cannot be stood against — and then call themselves a reminder. The response they ask for is not fascination with the details but the movement they were sent to produce: gratitude in place of al-Walid's ingratitude, and submission in place of the frown, the turned back and the raised chin.

passages.title: By the moon and the dawn: a warning to all
passages.tafsir:
Allah has just told the Quraysh that the keepers of the Fire are angels, that their number has been fixed as a trial, and that **none can know the hosts of your Lord but He** (ayah 31). They answered it with arithmetic. These six ayat are what follows: an oath — by the moon, by the retreating night, by the breaking dawn — that Hell is *one of the mightiest catastrophes*, a warning to humankind, addressed to whichever of them chooses to take the lead or lag behind.

Read in order, the shape is plain. Ayat 32–34 are the sworn witnesses. Ayah 35 is what is sworn to. Ayat 36 and 37 name who the warning is for and what it leaves in their hands.

## The taunt these ayat answer

To feel the force of "But no!" in ayah 32, you have to hear what was said just before it.

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah's words *And We have set none but angels as guardians of the Fire* are a refutation of the idolaters of the Quraysh when they mentioned the number of guardian angels. Abu Jahl said: "O people of Quraysh! Are not every ten among you able to defeat one of them?" Ibn Kathir's gloss on the ayah answers the arithmetic directly: these are guardian angels, stern and severe, "extremely strong in their creation. They cannot be stood against nor defeated."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second strand.
