Muqatil, among the leading authorities, says that the words *And no one knows the hosts of your Lord but He* (74:31) are a rebuttal to Abu Jahl's statement: when he heard the verse saying there are nineteen angels in charge of Hell, he addressed the youth of Quraysh and told them that the Prophet ﷺ has only nineteen companions, so there is nothing to worry about.

Two individual boasts are recorded in these sources. Ibn Kathir relates that it has been said that Abu Al-Ashaddayn — whose name was Kaladah bin Usayd bin Khalaf — said, "O people of Quraysh! You defend me against two of them and I will defend you against seventeen of them," saying it because he thought himself to be very great. They claimed of him that he had reached such strength that he would stand on a skin of cow hide and ten people would try to pull it out from under his feet, and the skin would be torn to pieces and still not be removed from under him. Separately, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Baihaqi records a narrative from Suddi: when verse 30 was revealed, a foolish Quraishi unbeliever, Abul-Asalain by name, spoke out, "O nation of Quraish, I alone am sufficient for the nineteen. I will take care of ten with my right arm, and nine with my left arm. Thus I will put an end to all nineteen of them."

That is the atmosphere. The nineteen had been mentioned, Ibn Kathir says, as a test: *We only have mentioned their number as being nineteen as a test from Us for mankind.* The same number that let the People of the Scripture arrive at certainty — knowing this Messenger is true, because he speaks according to the same thing they have with them of the heavenly revealed Scriptures that came to the Prophets before him — and made the believers increase in faith, made those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers say, "What does Allah intend by this example?" — that is, Ibn Kathir explains, "What is the wisdom in mentioning this here?" His comment on Allah's words *Thus Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills* is that by way of examples like this, faith becomes firm in the hearts of some people and is shaken with others; in this there is profound wisdom, and it is an irrefutable proof.

**Nineteen is not the size of the army.** Ibn Kathir stresses that *And none can know the hosts of your Lord but He* means none knows their number and their count except Allah — said, he adds, "so that one does not make the mistake of thinking that they are only nineteen in all." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the same point twice over: first of all, one angel is sufficient for them all; and moreover, the number nineteen refers to the chiefs of the angels — under each of these angels, the number of Allah's angels is legion beyond human count or computation, and Allah alone knows their number. They are ready at hand to carry out the punishment of the unbelievers and transgressors.

## From the Sunnah: a number no one can hold

Ibn Kathir brings, as confirmation, the Hadith concerning Al-Isra' that is reported in the Two Sahihs and other collections, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the Frequented House (Al-Bayt Al-Maʿmur), which is in the seventh heaven:

> Seventy thousand angels enter into it every day and they do not return to it as it is all that is due upon them (one visit in their lifetime).

Seventy thousand every day, and not one of them comes back. There is no arithmetic that catches up with that — and it is the arithmetic of Quraysh that these ayat are answering.

## "But no!" and the oath: the moon, the night, the dawn (ayat 32–34)

Ayah 32 opens with **كَلَّا** — given here as "But no!" and rendered by Ibn Kathir as "Nay!" Both renderings turn on a negative, and it stands exactly where the boasting stops and the oath begins.

Then come three sworn witnesses, and Ibn Kathir keeps his glosses plain:

- **By the moon** (ayah 32).
- **And by the night when it withdraws** — *idh adbara*, which Ibn Kathir explains as "when it withdraws" (ayah 33).
- **And by the dawn when it brightens** — *idhā asfara*, "when it shines" (ayah 34).

Notice what has been chosen. Not thrones or armies — the moon overhead, night pulling back, morning coming up bright. These are things every one of those men had watched a thousand times without effort or expense. The Quraysh were arguing about the unseen; the oath is sworn on what they can see any night they care to look up, and any morning they happen to be awake.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks the turn here simply: "In the next verses, there is the mention of the Hereafter and its horrors." The subject shifts from the guardians of the Fire to the Fire itself.

## What is sworn to (ayat 35–37)

*Innahā la-iḥdā al-kubar — nadhīran lil-bashar — liman shāʾa minkum an yataqaddama aw yataʾakhkhara.* One statement in three steps: what it is, who it is for, and what it leaves to them.

**"One of the mightiest catastrophes" (ayah 35).** What is the "it"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the pronoun in *innahā* refers to **Saqar** — Hell — which has been mentioned in one of the preceding verses. Ibn Kathir gives the same and names his authorities: this refers to the Hellfire, and Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and others of the Salaf all said this. Mujahid and others had already read the words of ayah 31, *And this is nothing but a reminder to mankind*, the same way: "this" means the Hellfire which has been described.

The Arabic repays a moment. **الكُبَر** (*al-kubar*), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, is a plural, and its singular is an adjective for a *dāhiyah* or *muṣībah* — a calamity, a disaster that falls on someone. So the sworn statement is not merely "Hell is great." It is: Hell is one of the greatest *calamities*. Ibn Kathir renders the sense as "the great things."

And hold on to that word **one**. *Iḥdā* — one of them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what that implies: the Hell that the unbelievers will enter will be one of the greatest calamities, and besides it there will be many different kinds of torments and tortures. The wording quietly refuses to let the reader treat this as the whole of the bad news.

**"A warning to humankind" (ayah 36).** The word **al-bashar** — human beings, humankind — has just been used in ayah 31: *And this is nothing but a reminder (dhikrā) to mankind*. Now the same audience is named again, and what was called a *reminder* is called a *warning*.

This matters against the backdrop of the story. The passage began with a specific quarrel among specific men in Makkah. It ends by widening to the whole species. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it plainly: the verse warns against the torment and torture of the Hellfire, and this applies to all human beings in general. Abu Jahl's arithmetic was the occasion; it was never the limit.

There is also mercy folded into the word *warning*. A warning is given before the thing arrives, to someone who still has time.

**"To whichever of you chooses to take the lead or lag behind" (ayah 37).** Two verbs: to go forward, and to hold back. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that in this context "to come forward" signifies coming forward towards faith and obedience, and *taʾakhkhur*, "to go backward," signifies moving away from faith and obedience. Ibn Kathir puts it in terms of the warning itself: this is for whoever wishes to accept the warning and be guided to the truth, or to hold back from accepting it, turn away from it and reject it.

Two things are worth noticing.

**First, the warning is the same for everyone; the response is not.** One announcement about nineteen angels brought the People of the Scripture to certainty, increased the believers in faith, and drew from others the question "What does Allah intend by this example?" As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises at this ayah: some accept the warning and are guided by the truth, and the unfortunate ones hold back from accepting the warning, turn away from it and reject it. The difference was never in the message.

**Second, the ayah addresses you as one who chooses** — *to whichever of you chooses*. Yet ayah 31 has just said that *Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills*, which Ibn Kathir explains as this: by way of examples like this one, faith becomes firm in the hearts of some people and is shaken with others — and in that there is profound wisdom, and an irrefutable proof. Both statements stand in the same passage, and both are to be received as Allah has given them; neither is set against the other. Ayah 37 is where our part of it sits, and it is put in the language of wishing and choosing.

## Living it

The passage does not end with information. It ends with a position: forward, or back.

- **Take the threat at the size the oath gives it.** Allah swore by the moon, the night and the dawn that this is *one of* the mightiest catastrophes — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that besides it there will be many different kinds of torments. The instinct to shrink it, to make it manageable and arithmetical, is the instinct on display in the boasts these ayat answer.
- **Be careful of counting where Allah has said you cannot count.** *And none can know the hosts of your Lord but He.* Ibn Kathir tells us why it was said: so that one does not make the mistake of thinking they are only nineteen in all. The mistake was confidence about something Allah had kept to Himself.
- **Ask which of the two verbs describes your last year.** *Yataqaddam* or *yataʾakhkhar* — coming forward towards faith and obedience, or moving away from faith and obedience. Those are the two directions the ayah names.
- **Hear a warning as a mercy while it is still a warning.** It is addressed to *al-bashar*, to human beings in general — which includes the one reading it now — and it arrives before the thing it warns about does.

passages.title: The people of the right question the guilty
passages.tafsir:
These eleven ayat move from a principle, to a scene, to a verdict. The principle: every soul is held as security against what it earned (38), with one group excepted (39). The scene: the saved, at ease in Gardens, put a question to the guilty in the Fire, and the guilty answer in their own words (40–47). The verdict: for people like this, no intercessor's plea will help (48).

What binds the passage into one unit is a single image — a **debt**. Ayah 38 says the soul is held in pawn against it. Ayat 43–46 are the debtors themselves reading out the list of what they never paid. Ayah 48 closes the last door by which the debt might have been written off.

## "Held in pledge" — the word rahīnah (38)

The word Allah chooses is **رَهِينَة (rahīnah)**, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains is used here in the sense of *marhūnah*, "will be detained." Its root is **رَهْن (rahn)** — to hand something valuable to a pawnbroker as security for a debt. Maʿārif draws out exactly what that means for the pawned object: it sits in the broker's keeping, and *he cannot use it or take advantage of it*. It is not destroyed; it is frozen. Held. Likewise, says Maʿārif, every person on the Day of Judgment will be detained in lieu of his sins.

So the ayah is not merely saying "everyone is responsible for what they did." It is saying that on that Day a person *is* the security lodged against his own record. Ibn Kathir gives the same sense more plainly: **"bound to his deed on the Day of Judgement,"** and he notes that this is what Ibn ʿAbbas and others said. Nothing external holds you there. Your own earnings are the lien.

Notice also **كَسَبَتْ (kasabat)** — "what it *earned*." Once Maʿārif has opened the pawnbroker's image, the whole vocabulary of the passage turns commercial: earning, security, detention, a debt repaid. It is a way of speaking that anyone who has ever owed money understands in the body.

## Except the People of the Right (39) — two readings

Ayah 39 carves out an exception: **أَصْحَاب الْيَمِين**, the People of the Right. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them as those who will be given their Book of Deeds in their right hands.

Maʿārif then lays out two ways of reading the "detention" of ayah 38, and the reasoning is worth following, not just the conclusion.

**First reading — detention *in Hell*.** Every person is held in pledge in Hell against his sins, to receive punishment; the People of the Right are excepted because they *have repaid the debt*. Maʿārif spells out what repayment means: they fulfilled their obligations in this world **towards Allah and towards other human beings**. A pledge is released when the loan is settled, so there is no need for them to be detained. Maʿārif calls this reading "plain, simple and straightforward."

**Second reading — detention at some other place**, before the accounting, or before admission into Paradise or Hell. On this reading, every person is held to give an account of his deeds, and no one is permitted to move out until his account is taken. But then the exception must mean something narrower: those not liable to accounting at all. Maʿārif mentions, as explained by Sayyidnā ʿAlī, the sinless — such as minors and immature children. It also mentions a Tradition that a segment of the Prophet's ﷺ community would be exempted from accountability and will enter Paradise without having to account for their actions; possibly the exception points to them. (The source names no collection for that report, so take it exactly as Maʿārif transmits it.)

Maʿārif raises one further difficulty with the second reading. Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah divides the people of the Plain of Gathering into three: the *sābiqūn* / *muqarrabūn* (the Foremost, those who have attained nearness to Allah), the People of the Right, and the People of the Left. Here in ayah 39 the *muqarrabūn* have been merged with the People of the Right and only the latter named — so there is no express text establishing that *all* the People of the Right are excepted from being detained for accountability. Maʿārif's own judgement: the first interpretation, being held in Hell, appropriately fits the context — and it closes where a careful scholar closes, **"And Allah knows best!"**

Either way, the warning stands: no one walks past the accounting simply by wishing to.

## A conversation across the whole distance of the Hereafter (40–42)

Ayah 40 places the saved **فِي جَنَّاتٍ يَتَسَاءَلُونَ** — "in Gardens, asking one another." Their asking turns to **الْمُجْرِمِين**, the guilty (41), and in ayah 42 they put the question to them directly.

Ibn Kathir fixes the geometry of the scene: the People of the Right are **in lofty rooms**, and from there they question the criminals, who are **in the lowest levels** of the Fire. The full vertical span of the Hereafter lies between the questioner and the questioned. And notice who is asking. Ibn Kathir heads the whole passage as *"the Discussion between the People of Paradise and the People of the Hellfire"* — not an angel, not a judge, but fellow human beings.

The question itself is short and devastating: **مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ** — "What has caused you to enter Hell?", or in the other rendering here, "What has landed you in Hell?" (The Arabic word both renderings translate as "Hell" is *Saqar*.) It is the simplest question anyone would ask: *how did you end up there?*

## The confession, in their own mouths (43–46)

No one testifies against them. They answer for themselves, and the answer is four items long. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān numbers them exactly: (1) they did not perform the obligatory prayers; (2) they did not feed the poor — that is, they did not spend on the necessities of the poor; (3) they indulged, in mocking at the truth, along with those who indulged in opposing Islam or in committing sins and shameful deeds; (4) they denied the Day of Requital.

**"We were not of those who prayed" (43) and "nor did we feed the poor" (44).** Ibn Kathir compresses these two into one sentence worth memorising: *"we did not worship Allah, nor did we do good to His creatures of our own species."* There it is — the two obligations Maʿārif named at ayah 39, the ones the People of the Right had discharged, itemised now by the debtors themselves. The right of Allah, and the right of human beings. Prayer is the plainest form of the first; feeding the poor the plainest form of the second — and Maʿārif keeps that second one concrete: spending on the *necessities* of the poor.

**"We used to indulge along with those who indulged" (45).** The verb is **نَخُوض (nakhūḍ)**, rendered here as indulging in falsehood, or "speaking falsehood with vain speakers." Ibn Kathir explains it as *"we used to speak about what we had no knowledge of."* Qatadah puts it as company rather than content: **"every time someone went astray we would go astray with them."** The ayah itself carries this in the word **مَعَ (maʿa)**, "along with" — the sin named is not an opinion held alone but a current joined. They went wherever the talk went.

**"And we used to deny the Day of Judgment" (46).** This is the fourth item, and it is the one Maʿārif singles out when it reaches ayah 48: whoever has these characteristics, *including denial of the Day of Requital*, is an infidel — one who has rejected faith outright. The other three are grave; this one settles the category of the whole list. Read alongside them it also makes sense of them, for a prayer, a poor man's meal and the weight of one's own words all mean something different to a person who is not expecting a Day of Requital at all.

## "Until the certainty came to us" (47)

**حَتَّىٰ أَتَانَا الْيَقِين** — "until *al-yaqīn* came to us." Ibn Kathir states plainly that al-yaqīn here means **death**, and brings the parallel from elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And worship your Lord until there comes unto you the certainty"* (15:99). He also cites the Prophet ﷺ saying of ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn that **al-yaqīn — death — had come to him from his Lord**. (The source names no collection for this report; it is given here as the source gives it.)

It is a bitterly exact name. These are people who spent a life denying the Day of Recompense — and the thing that ended the denial is called *the certainty*. And the small word *ḥattā*, "until," is where the confession turns tragic: they did not stop, revise, or repent. The list ran to the end of the line.

## "So no intercession of intercessors will benefit them" (48)

Ayah 48 draws the conclusion. Maʿārif notes that the attached pronoun in *tanfaʿuhum* ("benefit **them**") refers back to precisely these sinners, the ones who confessed those four crimes — and that a set of characteristics *including denial of the Day of Requital* amounts to disbelief. Ibn Kathir: whoever has these characteristics, the intercession of whoever tries to intercede for him will be of no benefit on the Day of Judgement, **"because intercession is only useful if the conditions for it are met."** Whoever comes before Allah on that Day as a disbeliever will have the Hellfire, with no way of avoiding it, abiding in it forever.

Then there is a detail of wording Maʿārif points out that is easy to skate over. Allah does not say "no intercessor will benefit them" but **شَفَاعَةُ الشَّافِعِين** — "the intercession *of the intercessors*," plural upon plural. Maʿārif reads the plural exactly so: *even if all the intercessors join forces to intercede*, it will not help. The refusal is not for want of anyone willing to plead.

## What intercession *does* avail — and for whom

Read from the other side, the same ayah is among the clearest proofs that intercession is real. Maʿārif draws the inference directly: besides those who reject faith, **all Muslims — even sinful ones — will benefit from intercession**, and many authentic aḥādīth bear ample testimony to this. The intercessors will be the Prophets of Allah, the friends of Allah, and righteous personalities; and it is confirmed that the general body of believers will intercede for one another, and that their intercession will be accepted.

Maʿārif then records a narration from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd: the angels of Allah and the Prophets, the martyrs and the righteous will intercede for sinners in the Hereafter and they will be delivered from Hell by virtue of that intercession — **except the four types of sinners classified in these ayat**: those who failed to perform the obligatory prayer and to pay Zakāh, those who opposed Islam alongside its opponents, and those who denied the Hereafter. Taken at face value, this shows that intercession will not be accepted for one who abandoned prayer and Zakāh.

But Maʿārif is careful here, and so should we be. It reports that other narratives indicate the correct view of this ayah: the unacceptability of intercession refers to sinners who commit these four crimes *together*, rejection of the Hereafter included. Apart from that rejection, it is not necessary that those committing the other sins be dealt with in the same way. Maʿārif adds that other hadith narratives do refer to certain major sins that deprive a person of intercession — for instance, denying the veracity of intercession, or denying the existence of the Pond of Kawthar: such a person will have no share in either. Where the scholars weigh reports against one another like this, the honest course is to hold firmly to what the ayah settles — that rejection of faith bars intercession absolutely — and to leave the disputed margin as they left it.

## Living it

**The list is unremarkable, and that is the point.** No murder is confessed in ayat 43–46, no theft. What ruins them is a prayer not prayed, a poor man not fed, a conversation joined, and a Day not taken seriously. These are sins of *drift* — omissions and company — exactly the sins a person can commit while thinking of himself as basically decent.

**Guard the two obligations.** Ibn Kathir's pairing gives a daily audit: worship of Allah, and good done to His creation. Salah for the first; feeding the poor — which Maʿārif glosses as spending on their actual necessities — for the second. Maʿārif says these are precisely the obligations, towards Allah and towards other human beings, that the People of the Right had already discharged. Ayah 38 says you are held against them until they are settled.

**Watch the company as closely as the creed.** Qatadah's reading of ayah 45 is uncomfortably modern: whenever a crowd went astray, they went astray with it. That is how most people are ruined — not by argument, but by drifting with whoever is talking.

**Do not bank on someone pleading for you.** Intercession is real and it is a mercy from Allah, but ayah 48 stands over anyone who means to lean on it while conceding these four counts. Intercession works when its conditions are met; it is not a route around faith and deeds, it is Allah's gift to those who had them.

**And the "until" of ayah 47 is still ahead of us, not behind.** For the people in that scene, the account ran on until *al-yaqīn* — death — arrived and closed it. It has not yet arrived for us. Ibn Kathir's parallel is where a believer should stand while it is still coming: **"And worship your Lord until there comes unto you the certainty"** (15:99). The same word that sealed their confession is the word that marks out the whole working length of a believing life.

passages.title: Fleeing the reminder like startled zebras
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Allah has just let us hear the people of the Fire explaining, in their own words, what put them there — Ibn Kathir heads that stretch of ayat "What will take place in the Discussion between the People of Paradise and the People of the Hellfire." Then the address turns. The section heading Ibn Kathir places over ayah 49 reads: "The Disapproval of the Disbelievers' Rejection and Their Position." Ayat 49–53 move as one unit: a question of disapproval (49), a picture (50–51), what they demand instead (52), and what Ibn Kathir identifies as the corruption underneath it all (53).

## Why ayah 49 begins with "So…"

The ayah opens with *fa-mā lahum* — "So what is the matter with them…" The "so" ties it to everything before it, and Ibn Kathir lays out that whole run of ayat together, from ayah 38 onward.

Every person is a pledge for what he has earned — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, "bound to his deed on the Day of Judgement," and he notes that "Ibn 'Abbas and others have said this." Except those on the Right: they will be in Gardens, and — while they are "in lofty rooms" — they will ask the criminals, "who will be in the lowest levels (of Hell)": "What has caused you to enter Hell?" (the Arabic of ayah 42 names the Fire as *Saqar*).

The criminals answer with four things (ayat 43–46): we were not of those who used to offer the Salah, nor did we feed the poor, we used to speak falsehood with vain speakers, and we used to deny the Day of Recompense — until *al-Yaqin*, the certainty, came to us. Ibn Kathir glosses the first two as: "we did not worship Allah, nor did we do good to His creatures of our own species (i.e., other people)." The third he glosses as "we used to speak about what we had no knowledge of," and records Qatadah's comment on it: "It means that every time someone went astray we would go astray with them." *Al-Yaqin*, he explains, means death, and he cites "And worship your Lord until there comes unto you the certainty" (15:99).

Then ayah 48: no intercession of intercessors will be of any use to them. Ibn Kathir explains why: "intercession is only useful if the conditions for it are met. However, whoever comes before Allah as a disbeliever on the Day of Judgement, then he will get the Hellfire and there is no way of avoiding it."

That is the ground ayah 49 stands on. Ibn Kathir renders the question this way: "what is wrong with these disbelievers who are turning away from what you are calling them to and reminding them of?"

Two things are worth noticing in that rendering. First, who is being addressed: the question is put to the Prophet ﷺ, about them, and it concerns *what he is calling them to*. Second, what Ibn Kathir calls the question in his heading — **disapproval**. This is not a request for information. It is a rebuke of their turning away.

## "The Reminder" — what exactly are they turning from?

The word in ayah 49 is *al-tadhkirah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word "in this context, refers to the Holy Qur'an, because the word literally signifies a 'reminder or something that reminds'."

And the surah defines its own term. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: "Towards the end, the verse 54 has explained that the 'Reminder' is the Holy Qur'an that is rejected by them." Ibn Kathir glosses ayah 54 in exactly those plain words — "truly the Qur'an is a reminder."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then names what makes the Qur'an unique as a reminder: "The Qur'an is unique in reminding Allah's attributes of perfection, His mercy and wrath, and the reward and punishment."

That short line is worth pausing over, because it tells us the *content* of what is being fled. Three things are named. Allah's attributes of perfection. His mercy and His wrath — held together, neither one alone. And reward and punishment, which is to say: consequences that are real. *That* is the Reminder they are turning away from.

## Ayat 50–51: the picture

Instead of continuing to argue, the ayat give an image: *ka'annahum ḥumurun mustanfirah, farrat min qaswarah*.

Ibn Kathir gives the meaning: "as if they were fleeing from the truth and turning away from it, like a wild donkey when it flees from something that is trying to catch it, like a lion." He notes: "This was said by Abu Hurayrah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the two ayat as describing "the allergy of the infidels against the Holy Qur'an."

**The animal.** Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both render *ḥumur* as "wild donkeys"; the translation on this page reads "spooked zebras." Either rendering carries the same thing: this is not calm, reasoned rejection being described. It is flight.

**The direction.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is precise about what is being fled from: they are "fleeing from the truth and turning away from it." The flight in the image is a flight *from the truth* — and, per Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, specifically from the Holy Qur'an. Their reaction is the reaction of an animal escaping a predator; its object is a Reminder.

### The word *qaswarah*

This is a rare and striking word, and the early authorities discussed it.

Ibn Kathir transmits it with a chain: Hammad bin Salamah reported from 'Ali bin Zayd, who reported from Yusuf bin Mihran, who narrated that **Ibn 'Abbas** said: "It (Qaswarah) is the lion in the Arabic language. It is called Qaswarah in the Abyssinian language, Sher in the Persian language and Awba in the Nabtiyyah (Nabatean) language."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that *qaswarah* carries **two** meanings: "[1] a 'lion'; and [2] an 'archer' or a 'hunter'." And it adds: "Both meanings have been reported from the noble Companions."

So this is a genuine difference among the early authorities, and it is reported as a difference rather than settled one way. Either way the shape of the image holds — something the herd flees from — and either way the flight is directed at what Ibn Kathir has already named: the truth.

## Ayah 52: what they want instead

*Bal yurīdu kullu-mri'in minhum an yu'tā ṣuḥufan munashsharah* — "In fact, each one of them wishes to be given a personal letter," pages spread out. The particle *bal* ("rather," "in fact") turns the sentence toward what they actually want.

Ibn Kathir explains, attributing it to **Mujahid** and others: "each one of these idolators wants to have a book revealed to him as Allah revealed to the Prophet ﷺ." He then cites a parallel from Surah al-An'am: "And when there comes to them a sign they say: 'We shall not believe until we receive the like of that which the Messengers of Allah had received.' Allah knows best with whom to place His Message" (6:124). That closing clause is where Ibn Kathir leaves it, and it is worth reading slowly: *Allah knows best with whom to place His Message.*

Ibn Kathir also records a second reading, in a narration from **Qatadah**: "They want to be declared innocent (on the Day of Judgement) without having to do any deeds."

Two readings, then, of what the "pages spread out" are: a personal revelation of one's own, or a personal acquittal without deeds. Ibn Kathir reports both.

## Ayah 53: the diagnosis

Then the correction: *kallā, bal lā yakhāfūna al-ākhirah* — "But no! In fact, they do not fear the Hereafter." *Kallā* is a word of rebuttal.

Ibn Kathir's comment is compact and decisive: "they were only corrupted by their lack of faith in it and their rejection of its occurrence."

That is the diagnosis the passage has been building toward, and it lets the whole unit be read backwards as a chain:

- They do not fear the Hereafter (53) — Ibn Kathir: this is what corrupted them —
- so instead of accepting the Reminder they want pages spread out to themselves (52) —
- so they turn from the truth as if fleeing from something hunting them (50–51) —
- and the disapproving question of ayah 49 has its answer.

The corruption is not located in a lack of evidence. Ibn Kathir places it in the heart's relationship to the Last Day.

## Living it

The people described here are, in Ibn Kathir's words, "these disbelievers" and "these idolators" — but the pattern the ayat expose is worth holding up against ourselves.

**Watch the reflex.** The image in ayat 50–51 is not of people who weighed the Qur'an and found it wanting. Ibn Kathir describes people "fleeing from the truth and turning away from it." When a reminder lands and something in us immediately reaches for the exit, that reflex is the thing ayah 49 puts its question to.

**Beware of wanting it on your own terms.** Both readings Ibn Kathir records of ayah 52 are versions of the same request: a private revelation of my own, or a clean verdict without deeds. Against the first stands the clause he quotes — "Allah knows best with whom to place His Message." Against the second stands Qatadah's plain description of what is being asked for: to "be declared innocent... without having to do any deeds."

**Fix the root, not the branch.** Ibn Kathir locates the whole corruption in the failure to fear the Hereafter. Notice that the very first things the people of the Fire admit to neglecting are Salah and feeding the poor — which Ibn Kathir glosses as worshipping Allah and doing good to His creatures. Where the Last Day is not real to a heart, those are the first two things to go.

**And the surah does not end on ayah 53.** Ibn Kathir carries straight on through the closing ayat: *kallā innahu tadhkirah* — "truly the Qur'an is a reminder" (54); "So, whosoever wills receives admonition from it" (55); "And they will not receive admonition unless Allah wills" (56), which he pairs with "And you cannot will unless Allah wills" (81:29). Both halves stand together as the ayat place them: a real human willing, and Allah's will, which nothing falls outside of. So we choose — and we ask Him for the choosing.

And the last words of the surah, as Ibn Kathir reports them from **Qatadah**, are the ones to walk away with: *He deserves to be feared and He is eligible to forgive the sin of whoever turns to Him and repents.*

passages.title: The Quran is a reminder for whoever wills
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Sūrah al-Muddaththir. After a long passage in which Allah exposes why people turn away from His message — and lets the people of the Fire describe their own ruin in their own words — the sūrah ends with an open hand: this Qur'an **is** the Reminder; take it, whoever wills. The three ayat move in one arc: a rebuttal that shuts down the excuse (54), an invitation left open to any human will (55), and then the will beneath it — Allah's own — followed by the sūrah's last words about Allah Himself, who alone is worthy to be feared and alone has the power to forgive (56).

## What ayah 54 is answering

Ayah 54 opens with a rebuttal, so it helps to know briefly what is being rebutted.

In the ayat just before, those on the Right, in Gardens and — as Ibn Kathir puts it — in lofty rooms, call down to the criminals in the lowest levels of Hell and ask what brought them there. The answer is a confession: we did not pray, we did not feed the poor, we spoke falsehood with vain speakers, and we denied the Day of Recompense. Ibn Kathir sums up the first two as *"we did not worship Allah, nor did we do good to His creatures of our own species"* — that is, other people. Of the third he says it means speaking about what they had no knowledge of; Qatādah's reading is that every time someone went astray, they went astray with them.

Then Allah asks (49) what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, what is wrong with these people who turn away from what you are calling them to and reminding them of? The answer comes as a picture: they flee the truth the way a wild donkey flees from something trying to catch it, like a lion. This was said by Abū Hurayrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *qaswarah* carries two reported meanings — a lion, and an archer or hunter — and that both are reported from the noble Companions.

Underneath the panic sits arrogance (52): each one of these idolaters wants a book revealed to **him**, as Allah revealed to the Prophet ﷺ — "Mujāhid and others have said this," Ibn Kathir writes, setting it beside *"We shall not believe until we receive the like of that which the Messengers of Allah had received"* (6:124). Qatādah's reported comment is sharper still: they want to be declared innocent on the Day of Judgement without having to do any deeds. And ayah 53 names the root — they do not fear the Hereafter — which Ibn Kathir explains as this: they were corrupted only by their lack of faith in it and their rejection of its occurrence.

So by the time we reach ayah 54, the diagnosis is finished. The problem was never a shortage of evidence.

## Ayah 54 — "Enough! Surely this is a reminder"

*kallā innahu tadhkirah* — **"Enough! Surely this ˹Qur'an˺ is a reminder."** Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"Nay, verily, this is an admonition."*

**Kallā** — "Enough!", "Nay" — is a word of rebuttal, and it answers the demand made in ayah 52: no, the Book you are asking to be handed privately is already in front of you.

Ibn Kathir's comment is deliberately plain: it means *"truly the Qur'an is a reminder."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same identification explicitly — the *tadhkirah* they were accused of turning away from in ayah 49 is the Holy Qur'an, and verse 54 "has explained that the 'Reminder' is the Holy Qur'an that is rejected by them."

**Why "reminder."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word simply: *tadhkirah* "literally signifies a 'reminder or something that reminds'." And it specifies what this Book is uniquely reminding us of — Allah's attributes of perfection, His mercy and His wrath, and the reward and the punishment. Those are precisely the things the person of ayah 53, the one who does not fear the Hereafter, has managed not to keep in view.

## Ayah 55 — the door left open

*fa-man shāʼa dhakarah* — **"So let whoever wills be mindful of it."** Ibn Kathir: *"So, whosoever wills receives admonition from it."*

Notice the shape of the sentence. There is no gatekeeper in it, no qualifying condition, no requirement that you first be given your own pages spread out. The address is simply to the will: *whoever wills*. After all those ayat describing people bolting from the Reminder, Allah states the terms and leaves the offer standing for anyone who wants it.

What "being mindful of it" looks like in practice, this same passage has already shown us in the negative. The people of the Fire name exactly what they left undone (43–46): the prayer, the poor, the tongue, the Day of Recompense. And Ibn Kathir's summary of the first pair — worshipping Allah, and doing good to other people — marks out the two directions that confession runs in.

There is also a sobering note standing beside the open offer. Ayah 48 says no intercession of intercessors will be of any use to them. Ibn Kathir is precise about why: intercession is only useful if the conditions for it are met; but whoever comes before Allah on the Day of Judgement as a disbeliever will get the Hellfire, with no way of avoiding it, abiding in it forever.

## Ayah 56 — "but they cannot do so unless Allah wills"

*wa mā yadhkurūna illā an yashāʼa Allāh* — **"But they cannot do so unless Allah wills."** The moment the door is opened to human will, Allah names His own will in the same breath.

Ibn Kathir's comment here is a single cross-reference. He sets the ayah beside its counterpart in the Qur'an: *"And you cannot will unless Allah wills"* (81:29). He does not expand on it, and it is better not to go further than he did — the ayah is stated, and its like in the Book is stated alongside it.

What the wording does put in front of the reader is this: if no one becomes mindful except by Allah's will, then the one who wants to be mindful knows exactly whom to ask.

## The sūrah's last words — *ahl at-taqwā*, *ahl al-maghfirah*

*huwa ahl at-taqwā wa ahl al-maghfirah.* The sūrah does not end with us. It ends with Him.

Ibn Kathir renders the phrase *"He is the One, deserving the Taqwa and He is the One Who forgives."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it *"He is worthy to be feared, and worthy to forgive."*

**Ahl at-taqwā.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Allah is *ahl at-taqwā* in the sense that "He alone is worthy to be feared and entitled to be obeyed." Note the second half of that gloss: not only feared, but obeyed. The two are named together in one breath.

**Ahl al-maghfirah.** Ibn Kathir gives Qatādah's comment on the phrase: it means that "He deserves to be feared and He is eligible to forgive the sin of whoever turns to Him and repents." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the exclusivity the phrase carries: *ahl al-maghfirah* signifies that "He alone is the Being Who forgives the sins of even the greatest sinners whenever He so wishes" — no one else has the power to do this.

Sit with the order of these two. A sūrah that has just described Saqar, the confession of the damned, the uselessness of intercession for the one who comes before Allah as a disbeliever, and people bolting like frightened donkeys from Allah's own Book — that sūrah ends by telling you that the One who is to be feared is also the only One with the power to forgive. Both are said about one Lord, in one line.

## Living it

- **Treat the Qur'an as what it calls itself.** Not a text to admire from a distance but a *tadhkirah* — something that reminds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names what it reminds us of: Allah's attributes of perfection, His mercy and His wrath, the reward and the punishment. Open it expecting to be reminded of those.
- **Do not wait for a private sign.** The demand of ayah 52 — my own pages spread out, then I will believe — is what this passage exposes, and Qatādah's reported comment names the wish underneath it: to be declared innocent without having to do any deeds.
- **Let the answer to "whoever wills" be yes.** Ayah 55 puts the offer directly to your will, with no condition attached to it.
- **Ask Allah for it.** Ayah 56 says they cannot do so unless Allah wills — so asking Him to make you one who remembers is the natural response to the ayah, not an afterthought.
- **Fear Him and hope in Him with the same heart.** He is *ahl at-taqwā* — worthy to be feared and entitled to be obeyed — and *ahl al-maghfirah* — the One who forgives the sins of even the greatest sinners when He so wills.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on this sūrah with the words *all praise and thanks are due to Allah*; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with *Alhamdulillah*. A fitting end to a sūrah whose closing word is forgiveness.
